audit.semantic_limit: Prose interpretation requires a separate source-based review.

body.statement: Coverage under the current spec is complete and matches across all names in the convenience sample: the only recorded exclusions are the warmup exclusions for insufficient trailing observations, no additional exclusions are recorded, the data-quality bundle reports no duplicate keys and no invalid or null closes, and each symbol's observed dates cover the full observed union. Within each symbol the eligible signals exceed the subset with a next observed close, because the final-row signal has no forward observation. Any added applicability rule, such as a volatility window or an absolute daily-return bound, can only remove eligible signals relative to this baseline, so its coverage cost must be justified from cited evidence.

citations.quote: All signal calculations use observations at/before t; execution no earlier than the next observed close.
Observed union is not an exchange calendar; absences are not proof of a market closure or suspension. No filling or corporate-action inference.
Close-only jumps cannot identify corporate actions.

body.statement: Timing is fixed by the source contract: every signal may use only closes observed at or before the signal close, and any execution cannot be earlier than the next observed close after the signal, which the final observed row of each symbol lacks. The observed date union is not an exchange calendar, so date absences are not proof of a market closure or suspension and no filling is permitted; return and volatility windows must be built from consecutive observed rows without interpolation. Close-only jumps cannot identify corporate actions, so an unusually large single-observation return must stay an unlabeled observation rather than being labeled a corporate event. Lengthening the lookback or adding a volatility window only postpones the first eligible signal inside the same observed sequence.

citations.quote: Normalization divides the trailing return by trailing daily-return SD times sqrt(lookback); this does not make an annual Sharpe ratio or remove systematic risk.

body.statement: Hypothesis: the unnormalized trailing-return score is not scale-comparable across names, because both the recorded one-observation return dispersion and the recorded baseline score dispersion differ materially across the sample; dividing the trailing return by the trailing daily-return standard deviation times the square root of the lookback may produce cross-symbol scores of more comparable magnitude. This remains unproven: the normalization consumes additional trailing observations and requires positive volatility, so it may shrink the eligible-signal set, and the source contract states the normalized score is not an annual Sharpe ratio and does not remove systematic risk. The needed next evidence is a comparative inspection of coverage and score scale for the normalized spec against the assigned baseline.

citations.quote: Descriptive score differences cannot establish superiority.

body.statement: Hypothesis: a majority of the symbols show negative mean raw trailing scores over this single window while the remaining symbol is near zero, and those negative means coincide with negative mean single-observation returns over the same period, so the sign pattern may reflect sample-period drift rather than short-horizon persistence; the observation nonetheless motivates an unproven reversal alternative, flipping the sign of the baseline direction, for later independent testing. Descriptive score differences cannot establish superiority, the names form a small convenience sample without a point-in-time universe, and no forward labels or performance evidence exist here, so neither the baseline direction nor the reversal can be preferred on current evidence; deciding evidence must come from a separate future evaluation.
